neighbours.label: describing a chemical reaction in progress or its observable products (reacts with, bubbles, gas produced)
fire: When the magnesium ribbon touches the acid, it fizzes and hydrogen gas is released.
Limestone reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, giving off carbon dioxide.
Adding sodium to water produces a violent reaction and a lot of heat.
In the second beaker a white precipitate formed as soon as the silver nitrate was added.
Iron slowly reacts with oxygen and moisture to form rust.
The students timed how long it took for the solution to stop releasing gas.
Copper carbonate decomposes on heating, leaving black copper oxide.
Vinegar and baking soda react to produce carbon dioxide bubbles.
quiet: The magnesium ribbon is stored in a labelled jar on the top shelf.
Limestone is a sedimentary rock quarried in many parts of England.
Sodium is kept under oil in the school's chemical cupboard.
In the second beaker the students poured exactly fifty millilitres of water.
Iron was used for tools long before steel became common.
The students recorded the temperature of the room before the lesson.
Copper carbonate is a green powder sold by laboratory suppliers.
Vinegar and baking soda are both common items in a kitchen cupboard.

notes: Card: chemistry tops (Ca(OH)2 + HCl, bubbles at the electrode, net-transfer reactions, chemical properties, gas produced, reacts with acid). Probe: 'bubbles of hydrogen' 0.94, cake bubbles 0.15. Near misses keep lab or chemistry settings but describe no reaction (storage, measurement, history).
